AI agents are becoming part of everyday software systems. They call APIs, retrieve information through MCP servers, use external tools, and delegate tasks to other agents. As these workflows become more capable, controlling what an agent can access and what it can do becomes a serious engineering concern, and it is the problem an agent gateway is built to solve.

An agent might need access to a customer database, an internal API, and an external model provider during the same workflow. Without a central control layer, teams can end up managing authentication, permissions, logging, and traffic policies across several independent integrations. That makes security reviews harder and leaves platform teams with limited visibility into what their agents are doing.

An agent gateway provides a shared layer for managing these interactions. It can authenticate agents, control access to tools, route requests, enforce policies, and record activity across agent-to-tool, agent-to-model, and agent-to-agent communication.

This guide compares nine agent gateways, including open-source projects, enterprise platforms, and managed cloud services. We'll look at their architecture, agent connectivity, security controls, deployment options, and pricing to help engineering teams identify the right fit for their AI infrastructure.

TL;DR

The best agent gateway depends on the protocols your agents use, the level of control your organization needs, and where you plan to run the gateway.

  • Bifrost: An open-source Go gateway for governing model requests, MCP tool calls, and agent-to-agent (A2A) traffic, with virtual keys, usage budgets, access controls, and low request overhead.
  • MuleSoft Agent Fabric: An enterprise platform for discovering, governing, and orchestrating AI agents, with centralized control over agent interactions, MCP connectivity, and A2A communication.
  • Kong AI Gateway: Extends Kong's API management platform with AI and agent traffic capabilities, including MCP access controls and agent-to-agent connectivity.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: A managed AWS gateway that exposes APIs, Lambda functions, and existing services as tools for agents, with authentication and routing for agentic traffic.
  • Google Cloud Agent Gateway: A managed gateway for governing agent communication over MCP, A2A, REST, and gRPC, with identity-aware access policies.
  • Azure AI Gateway: A Microsoft gateway for managing model APIs and MCP tools through centralized identity, policy enforcement, networking, and observability.
  • Gravitee: An API management platform with AI and agent gateway capabilities for governing LLM requests, MCP servers, and agent interactions.
  • IBM ContextForge: An open-source MCP gateway and registry for discovering, securing, and managing tools and services exposed to AI agents.
  • Agent Router: An open-source, Envoy-based gateway for routing AI and agent traffic across model providers, self-hosted inference, and MCP services.

Some of these products are purpose-built for agent traffic, while others extend existing API management or cloud infrastructure platforms. That distinction matters when comparing their features, deployment models, and licensing.

What Is an Agent Gateway, and Why Does It Matter?

An agent gateway is an infrastructure layer between AI agents and the resources they interact with. Those resources can include language models, APIs, MCP servers, databases, internal services, and other agents.

When an agent performs a task, it may make several calls across different systems. Each interaction can involve a different credential, permission level, protocol, or security requirement. An agent gateway gives platform teams a central place to manage those interactions and apply consistent controls.

Depending on the implementation, an agent gateway can provide:

  • Agent authentication and identity: Identify which agent is making a request and verify its credentials.
  • Tool access control: Restrict which MCP tools, APIs, and services an agent can invoke.
  • MCP traffic management: Route and govern requests between agents and Model Context Protocol servers.
  • Agent-to-agent communication: Manage interactions between agents using protocols such as A2A.
  • Model routing: Direct model requests to configured providers or inference services.
  • Observability and audit logs: Track tool calls, model requests, policy decisions, and agent activity.
  • Traffic and usage policies: Apply rate limits, quotas, and other controls to agent requests.

These capabilities become important when agents have access to business-critical systems. A permissions mistake can expose sensitive information, while an unmonitored tool call can trigger an unexpected operation or incur costs that are difficult to attribute.

An agent gateway helps establish a consistent security and governance layer around these interactions. It does not replace application-level authorization or make an agent inherently safe, but it gives infrastructure teams a central point to enforce and monitor important policies.

How We Evaluated These Agent Gateways

This comparison focuses on how well each platform handles the infrastructure requirements of real agentic applications. We considered the following criteria:

  • Agent and protocol support: Compatibility with MCP, A2A, model APIs, and other agent communication patterns.
  • Security and governance: Authentication, agent identity, authorization, tool-level permissions, and audit capabilities.
  • Traffic management: Routing, access policies, rate limits, quotas, and failure handling.
  • Deployment and integration: Self-hosted, managed, cloud-native, and enterprise deployment options.
  • Open-source availability and pricing: Which components are open source, what requires a commercial plan, and the operational costs involved.

The comparison distinguishes between products built specifically for agent connectivity and broader API or cloud platforms that provide agent gateway functionality.

The products differ in what they govern. Some focus on securing tool access and MCP connections, while others also handle model routing and agent-to-agent communication. The following sections discuss those differences in more detail.

1. Bifrost (by Maxim AI)

Bifrost is an open-source AI gateway built in Go that also provides MCP gateway and agent gateway capabilities. It gives AI applications and agents a unified interface for accessing model providers and external tools, with centralized routing, authentication, usage controls, and observability.

For teams building agentic applications, one of Bifrost's important capabilities is its MCP integration. Agents can access external tools through a managed gateway, while engineering teams control which tools are available and how requests are governed. Bifrost also supports more than 20 model providers through a consistent API, making it useful for applications that combine model calls with external tool execution.

MCP Gateway and Agent Tool Governance

An AI agent often needs access to several tools to complete a task. Managing those connections independently can make it difficult to enforce consistent permissions across applications and teams.

Bifrost provides an MCP gateway that connects agents to external MCP servers and applies centralized controls to tool access. Its virtual keys can define which MCP clients and tools an agent is allowed to use, giving teams a way to restrict access at the gateway level.

Key capabilities include:

  • MCP tool filtering: Control which tools are available to individual virtual keys.
  • Centralized tool access: Connect agents to external MCP servers through a managed gateway.
  • Federated authentication: Support authenticated access to internal APIs exposed through MCP.
  • MCP Code Mode: Let agents interact with multiple tools through code execution, reducing the overhead associated with handling large tool definitions and repeated calls.

This approach is useful when several agents or applications share the same internal tools but need different access permissions.

Agent Gateway (A2A)

Bifrost also provides a dedicated A2A Agent Gateway for managing communication between AI agents. Teams can register existing A2A agents and control which callers are allowed to reach each one, creating a centralized access layer for agent-to-agent interactions.

The gateway also supports credential forwarding and push notifications, helping agents communicate with existing services while preserving the authentication context required by those integrations. Bifrost links A2A tasks with their corresponding LLM and MCP logs, giving teams a more complete view of agent workflows.

For observability, agent telemetry can also be exported through OpenTelemetry, making it easier to monitor A2A activity alongside other AI traffic.

Performance, Routing, and Reliability

Agent workflows can generate several model and tool requests during a single user interaction. Gateway overhead can accumulate across those calls, making request performance an important infrastructure consideration.

Bifrost is written in Go and is designed to handle high-throughput AI traffic with low overhead. It adds 11 microseconds of overhead per request at 5,000 requests per second (RPS) on a t3.xlarge instance, with a 100% success rate in sustained benchmarks.

For production agent systems, Bifrost provides:

  • Automatic failover: Redirect requests when a configured provider becomes unavailable.
  • Adaptive load balancing: Distribute traffic across configured providers and API keys.
  • Retries and circuit breakers: Handle transient errors and provider degradation.
  • Semantic caching: Reuse eligible responses to reduce repeated model requests.

These capabilities help teams maintain predictable model access as agent workloads increase.

Observability, Access Control, and Cost Governance

When agents interact with internal services and external tools, teams need visibility into both AI consumption and the permissions granted to each application.

Bifrost uses virtual keys as a central governance mechanism. Each key can carry its own model access permissions, budget, and rate limits, allowing teams to associate AI usage with specific applications, customers, or workloads.

Its governance capabilities include:

  • Independent budgets: Set spending limits for individual virtual keys.
  • Rate limits: Apply token-based and request-based restrictions.
  • Model and provider filtering: Restrict which models and provider credentials a key can access.
  • MCP permissions: Control which configured tools are available to a key.
  • Observability: Use built-in dashboards and OpenTelemetry support to monitor AI traffic.

This gives platform teams a way to manage model usage and agent tool permissions through the same gateway infrastructure.

Pricing:

Bifrost's core gateway is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and can be self-hosted without a gateway license fee. Teams remain responsible for infrastructure costs and charges from the model providers they use.

Its Enterprise offering adds advanced capabilities such as RBAC, SSO, guardrails, audit logs, and private deployment options, including in-VPC, on-premises, and air-gapped environments.

Best for:

Engineering and platform teams building production AI agents that need centralized MCP tool governance, low-overhead model access, and control over usage across applications. It is a strong fit for organizations that want LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic governed through one low-overhead gateway, with self-hosted, in-VPC, or air-gapped deployment.

2. MuleSoft Agent Fabric

MuleSoft Agent Fabric is an enterprise platform for discovering, managing, and governing AI agents across an organization. It brings agent management and orchestration into the broader MuleSoft ecosystem, helping teams connect agents with enterprise APIs, systems, and business processes.

A central part of the platform is its approach to agent governance. Organizations can discover and register agents, manage their interactions, and apply governance policies across agent environments. Its support for MCP and A2A helps connect agents with tools and services while enabling communication between different agents.

MuleSoft Agent Fabric is designed for enterprises that need visibility and control as agent deployments grow across teams and business units. Its integration with MuleSoft's API management and connectivity capabilities also makes it relevant for organizations that already use MuleSoft to expose and manage enterprise services.

Pricing:

MuleSoft Agent Fabric is part of Salesforce's commercial enterprise platform. Pricing depends on the products, capabilities, and deployment requirements selected. Contact Salesforce or MuleSoft for a quote.

Best for:

Large organizations managing multiple AI agents across enterprise systems that need centralized discovery, governance, orchestration, and integration with existing APIs.

Explore MuleSoft Agent Fabric

3. Kong AI Gateway

Kong AI Gateway extends Kong's API connectivity and management platform to cover AI applications and multi-agent systems. It provides a centralized layer for governing LLM requests, MCP tool access, and agent-to-agent communication.

One of its main advantages is that it brings AI traffic management into an established API gateway ecosystem. Teams can expose existing APIs as MCP tools, aggregate tools from different sources, and apply authentication and access policies to how agents discover and invoke them.

Kong also supports A2A traffic through dedicated AI Agent entities. These allow teams to route agent requests and apply authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and observability policies. Administrators can monitor agent activity, including request latency, errors, and other telemetry, through Kong's management and observability capabilities.

For organizations already using Kong to manage APIs, this creates a familiar path to governing agent infrastructure without introducing a completely separate connectivity platform.

Pricing:

Kong offers an AI Management Plus plan starting at $25 per month, plus usage, with a free trial. Its Enterprise plan uses custom pricing and adds capabilities for larger deployments.

Best for:

Organizations already using Kong for API management, as well as enterprises that need centralized governance across LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic. It is especially relevant when agents need controlled access to existing enterprise APIs and services.

Explore Kong AI Gateway

4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is a managed gateway service designed to connect AI agents with tools, APIs, and existing services. It helps developers expose backend capabilities through a standardized interface that agents can discover and invoke using the Model Context Protocol.

A key use case is turning existing REST APIs, AWS Lambda functions, and other services into MCP-compatible tools. This allows teams to make existing business logic available to agents without building a separate tool integration for every application. AgentCore Gateway can also connect to existing MCP servers and support agent-to-agent communication through passthrough targets.

Because it is part of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the gateway fits naturally into AWS-based agent architectures. Teams can use it alongside other AgentCore capabilities to build and operate agents that interact with enterprise systems and external services.

The managed approach also reduces the infrastructure work involved in running a dedicated gateway. Developers can focus on configuring targets, permissions, and agent integrations while AWS manages the underlying service.

Pricing:

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway uses pay-as-you-go pricing. AWS lists gateway API invocations at $0.005 per 1,000 invocations, with additional charges for features such as search and tool indexing. Other AgentCore services and the AWS resources used by connected tools can generate separate costs.

Best for:

Teams building agents within the AWS ecosystem that need a managed way to expose APIs, Lambda functions, and existing services as MCP tools. It is a practical option for organizations that want to integrate agent capabilities with their existing AWS infrastructure.

Explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

5. Google Cloud Agent Gateway

Google Cloud Agent Gateway is a managed gateway within Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It provides a centralized layer for securing and governing communication between AI agents, tools, and backend services across cloud environments.

The gateway supports several agent communication protocols, including MCP, A2A, REST, and gRPC. This allows organizations to manage tool calls, agent delegation, and traditional service requests through a consistent gateway infrastructure. For MCP traffic, it can inspect JSON-RPC requests to identify tool names and methods, enabling more granular access policies.

Google Cloud Agent Gateway is designed for organizations that need to govern agent interactions across different deployment environments. It supports deployments involving Google Kubernetes Engine and Cloud Run, as well as cross-cloud scenarios. Its integration with Google Cloud's agent infrastructure also makes it relevant for teams already using Gemini and other Google Cloud services.

Pricing:

Google Cloud Agent Gateway is part of the managed Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Pricing depends on the selected deployment model and associated platform resources.

Best for:

Organizations building agents on Google Cloud that need centralized control over MCP tools, A2A communication, and backend service access. It is a strong option for teams managing agent workloads across GKE, Cloud Run, and hybrid or cross-cloud environments.

Explore Google Cloud Agent Gateway

6. Azure AI Gateway

Azure AI Gateway is Microsoft's managed gateway for connecting applications and AI agents to model providers, MCP servers, and other tools. It gives developers a shared endpoint for AI services while allowing platform teams to manage access, policies, networking, and observability centrally.

The gateway supports multiple model providers through familiar API interfaces, helping applications work with different models without requiring a separate integration for each provider. It can also publish MCP servers, OpenAPI APIs, and SaaS connectors through a unified MCP endpoint, making approved tools available to agents through a governed access layer.

For enterprise environments, Azure AI Gateway provides policies for access control, safety, token usage, and request rates. Its monitoring capabilities expose information such as token consumption, latency, errors, and policy outcomes. Integration with Azure identity and networking services also makes it suitable for organizations with established Microsoft security and infrastructure requirements.

Pricing:

Azure AI Gateway is currently offered as a preview service. Microsoft has not announced final pricing for the separate Azure API Management AI Gateway tier.

Best for:

Enterprises using Microsoft Azure that need a shared gateway for model APIs and MCP tools. It is especially useful for platform teams that want consistent identity, security policies, and monitoring across AI applications.

Explore Azure AI Gateway

7. Gravitee AI Gateway

Gravitee AI Gateway is part of Gravitee's API and agent management platform. It provides a unified runtime for governing LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic, helping organizations secure interactions across agents, models, tools, and existing APIs.

Gravitee separates these interactions into protocol-aware gateway components. Its LLM Proxy manages model requests, while its MCP Proxy controls tool discovery and invocation. The A2A Proxy governs communication between agents, including delegated requests and authorization across agent workflows.

A key distinction is its focus on fine-grained governance. Teams can apply policies to specific MCP methods, tools, and agent skills, with OAuth 2.1 authentication and delegated authorization support. Gravitee also connects observability across these interactions through OpenTelemetry, giving teams visibility into agent identities, tool usage, policy decisions, and request traces.

The platform also includes MCP Studio, which helps teams assemble composite MCP servers from existing APIs, tools, and other resources. This allows organizations to provide agents with curated tool collections while applying access policies at the composite level.

Pricing:

Gravitee offers commercial platform plans with pricing based on deployment requirements and selected capabilities. Its AI Gateway capabilities are part of its broader platform offering. Contact Gravitee for a quote and confirmation of the features available under each plan.

Best for:

Enterprises that need detailed governance across LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic. Gravitee is a good fit for organizations managing many agents and tools that require centralized authentication, fine-grained authorization, and end-to-end observability.

Explore Gravitee AI Gateway

8. IBM ContextForge

IBM ContextForge is an open-source MCP gateway and registry designed to help organizations manage tools, resources, and prompts across multiple MCP servers. It provides a centralized layer where AI agents can discover and access approved capabilities without requiring every application to maintain separate connections to individual services.

ContextForge supports MCP server federation, allowing teams to register and aggregate tools from different sources through a unified endpoint. It also provides authentication and authorization mechanisms, including OAuth-based access, JWT authentication, and role-based access control. Administrators can manage tool visibility, control access, and monitor interactions across connected services.

The platform also includes an administrative interface and observability integrations that help teams manage their MCP infrastructure. Its focus is on organizing and governing tool access, making it useful for organizations with growing MCP deployments that need a shared registry and gateway.

Pricing:

IBM ContextForge is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and can be self-hosted without a software license fee. Organizations can use their own infrastructure and configure the gateway according to their requirements.

Best for:

Teams building MCP-based agent environments that need a centralized tool registry, server federation, and access management. It is a practical option for organizations that prefer open-source infrastructure and want control over their MCP deployments.

Explore IBM ContextForge

9. Agent Router

Agent Router is an open-source gateway built on Envoy that helps teams manage traffic across AI models, agents, and tools. It provides a unified routing layer for applications that interact with multiple model providers and agent infrastructure.

The gateway is designed to simplify connectivity across different AI backends, including hosted model APIs and self-hosted inference services. It also supports MCP integration, allowing agent applications to connect with external tools through a centralized infrastructure layer.

By using Envoy as its underlying proxy, Agent Router fits into cloud-native environments where teams already rely on service proxies and infrastructure-level traffic management. This makes it relevant for platform engineers who want to bring AI traffic into their existing networking and observability architecture.

Pricing:

Agent Router is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Teams can self-host it without paying a software license fee, although infrastructure and operational costs still apply.

Best for:

Engineering teams that want an open-source, Envoy-based gateway for routing AI traffic across model providers and agent tools. It is worth evaluating for organizations that already use Envoy or need a customizable gateway within a cloud-native infrastructure stack.

How to Choose the Right Agent Gateway

The best agent gateway depends on how your agents communicate, which tools they need, and how much control your organization requires over their interactions. A gateway designed mainly for model routing may not provide the same capabilities as one built around MCP federation, A2A communication, or enterprise identity management.

  • Identifying the protocols your applications use

If your agents rely heavily on MCP servers, prioritize gateways with tool discovery, invocation controls, and authentication support. If your architecture includes multiple cooperating agents, check for A2A support and policies that govern agent-to-agent requests.

  • Security and governance should also influence your decision**

Look for granular permissions, identity-aware access, rate limits, audit logs, and visibility into tool usage. These capabilities become important as more agents gain access to internal APIs, customer data, and business systems.

  • Deployment requirements can narrow the list further

A managed service can reduce infrastructure maintenance, while an open-source, self-hosted gateway gives teams more control over configuration and deployment. Consider your existing cloud environment, Kubernetes setup, compliance requirements, and operational resources before choosing.

  • Evaluate performance and total cost

Agent workflows can generate multiple model and tool calls for a single task, so request overhead, retries, caching, and provider failover can affect both latency and spending. Test the gateway with realistic workloads and compare the cost of the gateway, infrastructure, model usage, and supporting services.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between an agent gateway and an LLM gateway?
An LLM gateway primarily manages requests between applications and language models. It handles model routing, provider selection, authentication, rate limits, and usage monitoring.
An agent gateway covers a broader set of interactions. It can govern communication between agents, tools, MCP servers, and model providers. Some platforms combine both capabilities, allowing teams to manage model requests and agent workflows through one infrastructure layer.
Why do AI agents need a gateway?
AI agents often access multiple tools, APIs, and services to complete tasks. Without centralized controls, each integration can introduce separate authentication, permission, monitoring, and security requirements.
A gateway provides a shared enforcement point for these interactions. It helps teams manage tool access, apply policies, monitor requests, and maintain visibility into how agents use connected resources.
What is the difference between MCP and A2A?
MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools, resources, and prompts. It provides a common interface for agents to discover and use capabilities exposed by MCP servers.
A2A (Agent2Agent) focuses on communication between independent AI agents. It allows agents to discover other agents, delegate tasks, and exchange information. Both protocols support different parts of an agentic architecture.
Can an agent gateway secure access to internal APIs?
Yes. An agent gateway can sit between agents and internal services, enforcing authentication, authorization, and access policies before requests reach backend resources.
Depending on the platform, teams can expose existing APIs as MCP tools, restrict access to specific operations, and monitor requests. Backend services should still enforce their own authorization and data-access rules, since gateway policies are one layer of a broader security architecture.
Should I choose an open-source or managed agent gateway?
An open-source gateway is a good choice when your team needs deployment flexibility, infrastructure control, and the ability to customize its configuration. It can also reduce software licensing costs, although your team remains responsible for hosting, maintenance, and operations.
A managed gateway can reduce operational overhead and integrate with an existing cloud ecosystem. It may be a better fit when your organization prefers a provider-managed service and already relies on that provider's identity, networking, and monitoring tools.

Final Thoughts

Agent gateways are becoming an important part of production AI infrastructure as applications gain access to more tools, services, and other agents. They give engineering teams a central place to manage communication, enforce access policies, monitor usage, and maintain control over increasingly complex agent workflows.

The nine platforms in this comparison address different needs. Bifrost covers LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic in a single open-source gateway, with enterprise governance and in-VPC, on-premises, or air-gapped deployment. Agent Router and IBM ContextForge are also worth evaluating for open-source deployments. Kong and Gravitee offer broader API management and agent governance capabilities, while Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, Google Cloud Agent Gateway, and Azure AI Gateway fit naturally into their respective cloud ecosystems. MuleSoft Agent Fabric provides enterprise agent discovery, orchestration, and governance.

Before choosing, test the gateway against your actual agent workflows. Check how it handles tool permissions, identity, protocol support, request volume, and failure scenarios.

Teams evaluating AI gateways can request a Bifrost demo or review the open-source repository.

This approach is useful when several agents or applications share the same internal tools but need different access permissions. Agent Gateway (A2A) Bifrost also provides a dedicated A2A Agent Gateway for managing communication between AI agents. Teams can register existing A2A agents and control which callers are allowed to reach each one, creating a centralized access layer for agent-to-agent interactions. The gateway also supports credential forwarding and push notifications, helping agents communicate with existing services while preserving the authentication context required by those integrations. Bifrost links A2A tasks with their corresponding LLM and MCP logs, giving teams a more complete view of agent workflows. For observability, agent telemetry can also be exported through OpenTelemetry, making it easier to monitor A2A activity alongside other AI traffic. Performance, Routing, and Reliability Agent workflows can generate several model and tool requests during a single user interaction. Gateway overhead can accumulate across those calls, making request performance an important infrastructure consideration. Bifrost is written in Go and is designed to handle high-throughput AI traffic with low overhead. It adds 11 microseconds of overhead per request at 5,000 requests per second (RPS) on a t3.xlarge instance, with a 100% success rate in sustained benchmarks. For production agent systems, Bifrost provides: Automatic failover: Redirect requests when a configured provider becomes unavailable. Adaptive load balancing: Distribute traffic across configured providers and API keys. Retries and circuit breakers: Handle transient errors and provider degradation. Semantic caching: Reuse eligible responses to reduce repeated model requests. These capabilities help teams maintain predictable model access as agent workloads increase. Observability, Access Control, and Cost Governance When agents interact with internal services and external tools, teams need visibility into both AI consumption and the permissions granted to each application. Bifrost uses virtual keys as a central governance mechanism. Each key can carry its own model access permissions, budget, and rate limits, allowing teams to associate AI usage with specific applications, customers, or workloads. Its governance capabilities include: Independent budgets: Set spending limits for individual virtual keys. Rate limits: Apply token-based and request-based restrictions. Model and provider filtering: Restrict which models and provider credentials a key can access. MCP permissions: Control which configured tools are available to a key. Observability: Use built-in dashboards and OpenTelemetry support to monitor AI traffic. This gives platform teams a way to manage model usage and agent tool permissions through the same gateway infrastructure. Pricing: Bifrost's core gateway is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and can be self-hosted without a gateway license fee. Teams remain responsible for infrastructure costs and charges from the model providers they use. Its Enterprise offering adds advanced capabilities such as RBAC, SSO, guardrails, audit logs, and private deployment options, including in-VPC, on-premises, and air-gapped environments. Best for: Engineering and platform teams building production AI agents that need centralized MCP tool governance, low-overhead model access, and control over usage across applications. It is a strong fit for organizations that want LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic governed through one low-overhead gateway, with self-hosted, in-VPC, or air-gapped deployment. Explore Bifrost 2. MuleSoft Agent Fabric MuleSoft Agent Fabric is an enterprise platform for discovering, managing, and governing AI agents across an organization. It brings agent management and orchestration into the broader MuleSoft ecosystem, helping teams connect agents with enterprise APIs, systems, and business processes. A central part of the platform is its approach to agent governance. Organizations can discover and register agents, manage their interactions, and apply governance policies across agent environments. Its support for MCP and A2A helps connect agents with tools and services while enabling communication between different agents. MuleSoft Agent Fabric is designed for enterprises that need visibility and control as agent deployments grow across teams and business units. Its integration with MuleSoft's API management and connectivity capabilities also makes it relevant for organizations that already use MuleSoft to expose and manage enterprise services. Pricing: MuleSoft Agent Fabric is part of Salesforce's commercial enterprise platform. Pricing depends on the products, capabilities, and deployment requirements selected. Contact Salesforce or MuleSoft for a quote. Best for: Large organizations managing multiple AI agents across enterprise systems that need centralized discovery, governance, orchestration, and integration with existing APIs. Explore MuleSoft Agent Fabric 3. Kong AI Gateway Kong AI Gateway extends Kong's API connectivity and management platform to cover AI applications and multi-agent systems. It provides a centralized layer for governing LLM requests, MCP tool access, and agent-to-agent communication. One of its main advantages is that it brings AI traffic management into an established API gateway ecosystem. Teams can expose existing APIs as MCP tools, aggregate tools from different sources, and apply authentication and access policies to how agents discover and invoke them. Kong also supports A2A traffic through dedicated AI Agent entities. These allow teams to route agent requests and apply authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and observability policies. Administrators can monitor agent activity, including request latency, errors, and other telemetry, through Kong's management and observability capabilities. For organizations already using Kong to manage APIs, this creates a familiar path to governing agent infrastructure without introducing a completely separate connectivity platform. Pricing: Kong offers an AI Management Plus plan starting at $25 per month, plus usage, with a free trial. Its Enterprise plan uses custom pricing and adds capabilities for larger deployments. Best for: Organizations already using Kong for API management, as well as enterprises that need centralized governance across LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic. It is especially relevant when agents need controlled access to existing enterprise APIs and services. Explore Kong AI Gateway 4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is a managed gateway service designed to connect AI agents with tools, APIs, and existing services. It helps developers expose backend capabilities through a standardized interface that agents can discover and invoke using the Model Context Protocol. A key use case is turning existing REST APIs, AWS Lambda functions, and other services into MCP-compatible tools. This allows teams to make existing business logic available to agents without building a separate tool integration for every application. AgentCore Gateway can also connect to existing MCP servers and support agent-to-agent communication through passthrough targets. Because it is part of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the gateway fits naturally into AWS-based agent architectures. Teams can use it alongside other AgentCore capabilities to build and operate agents that interact with enterprise systems and external services. The managed approach also reduces the infrastructure work involved in running a dedicated gateway. Developers can focus on configuring targets, permissions, and agent integrations while AWS manages the underlying service. Pricing: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway uses pay-as-you-go pricing. AWS lists gateway API invocations at $0.005 per 1,000 invocations, with additional charges for features such as search and tool indexing. Other AgentCore services and the AWS resources used by connected tools can generate separate costs. Best for: Teams building agents within the AWS ecosystem that need a managed way to expose APIs, Lambda functions, and existing services as MCP tools. It is a practical option for organizations that want to integrate agent capabilities with their existing AWS infrastructure. Explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway 5. Google Cloud Agent Gateway Google Cloud Agent Gateway is a managed gateway within Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It provides a centralized layer for securing and governing communication between AI agents, tools, and backend services across cloud environments. The gateway supports several agent communication protocols, including MCP, A2A, REST, and gRPC. This allows organizations to manage tool calls, agent delegation, and traditional service requests through a consistent gateway infrastructure. For MCP traffic, it can inspect JSON-RPC requests to identify tool names and methods, enabling more granular access policies. Google Cloud Agent Gateway is designed for organizations that need to govern agent interactions across different deployment environments. It supports deployments involving Google Kubernetes Engine and Cloud Run, as well as cross-cloud scenarios. Its integration with Google Cloud's agent infrastructure also makes it relevant for teams already using Gemini and other Google Cloud services. Pricing: Google Cloud Agent Gateway is part of the managed Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Pricing depends on the selected deployment model and associated platform resources. Best for: Organizations building agents on Google Cloud that need centralized control over MCP tools, A2A communication, and backend service access. It is a strong option for teams managing agent workloads across GKE, Cloud Run, and hybrid or cross-cloud environments. Explore Google Cloud Agent Gateway 6. Azure AI Gateway Azure AI Gateway is Microsoft's managed gateway for connecting applications and AI agents to model providers, MCP servers, and other tools. It gives developers a shared endpoint for AI services while allowing platform teams to manage access, policies, networking, and observability centrally. The gateway supports multiple model providers through familiar API interfaces, helping applications work with different models without requiring a separate integration for each provider. It can also publish MCP servers, OpenAPI APIs, and SaaS connectors through a unified MCP endpoint, making approved tools available to agents through a governed access layer. For enterprise environments, Azure AI Gateway provides policies for access control, safety, token usage, and request rates. Its monitoring capabilities expose information such as token consumption, latency, errors, and policy outcomes. Integration with Azure identity and networking services also makes it suitable for organizations with established Microsoft security and infrastructure requirements. Pricing: Azure AI Gateway is currently offered as a preview service. Microsoft has not announced final pricing for the separate Azure API Management AI Gateway tier. Best for: Enterprises using Microsoft Azure that need a shared gateway for model APIs and MCP tools. It is especially useful for platform teams that want consistent identity, security policies, and monitoring across AI applications. Explore Azure AI Gateway 7. Gravitee AI Gateway Gravitee AI Gateway is part of Gravitee's API and agent management platform. It provides a unified runtime for governing LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic, helping organizations secure interactions across agents, models, tools, and existing APIs. Gravitee separates these interactions into protocol-aware gateway components. Its LLM Proxy manages model requests, while its MCP Proxy controls tool discovery and invocation. The A2A Proxy governs communication between agents, including delegated requests and authorization across agent workflows. A key distinction is its focus on fine-grained governance. Teams can apply policies to specific MCP methods, tools, and agent skills, with OAuth 2.1 authentication and delegated authorization support. Gravitee also connects observability across these interactions through OpenTelemetry, giving teams visibility into agent identities, tool usage, policy decisions, and request traces. The platform also includes MCP Studio, which helps teams assemble composite MCP servers from existing APIs, tools, and other resources. This allows organizations to provide agents with curated tool collections while applying access policies at the composite level. Pricing: Gravitee offers commercial platform plans with pricing based on deployment requirements and selected capabilities. Its AI Gateway capabilities are part of its broader platform offering. Contact Gravitee for a quote and confirmation of the features available under each plan. Best for: Enterprises that need detailed governance across LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic. Gravitee is a good fit for organizations managing many agents and tools that require centralized authentication, fine-grained authorization, and end-to-end observability. Explore Gravitee AI Gateway 8. IBM ContextForge IBM ContextForge is an open-source MCP gateway and registry designed to help organizations manage tools, resources, and prompts across multiple MCP servers. It provides a centralized layer where AI agents can discover and access approved capabilities without requiring every application to maintain separate connections to individual services. ContextForge supports MCP server federation, allowing teams to register and aggregate tools from different sources through a unified endpoint. It also provides authentication and authorization mechanisms, including OAuth-based access, JWT authentication, and role-based access control. Administrators can manage tool visibility, control access, and monitor interactions across connected services. The platform also includes an administrative interface and observability integrations that help teams manage their MCP infrastructure. Its focus is on organizing and governing tool access, making it useful for organizations with growing MCP deployments that need a shared registry and gateway. Pricing: IBM ContextForge is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and can be self-hosted without a software license fee. Organizations can use their own infrastructure and configure the gateway according to their requirements. Best for: Teams building MCP-based agent environments that need a centralized tool registry, server federation, and access management. It is a practical option for organizations that prefer open-source infrastructure and want control over their MCP deployments. Explore IBM ContextForge 9. Agent Router Agent Router is an open-source gateway built on Envoy that helps teams manage traffic across AI models, agents, and tools. It provides a unified routing layer for applications that interact with multiple model providers and agent infrastructure. The gateway is designed to simplify connectivity across different AI backends, including hosted model APIs and self-hosted inference services. It also supports MCP integration, allowing agent applications to connect with external tools through a centralized infrastructure layer. By using Envoy as its underlying proxy, Agent Router fits into cloud-native environments where teams already rely on service proxies and infrastructure-level traffic management. This makes it relevant for platform engineers who want to bring AI traffic into their existing networking and observability architecture. Pricing: Agent Router is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Teams can self-host it without paying a software license fee, although infrastructure and operational costs still apply. Best for: Engineering teams that want an open-source, Envoy-based gateway for routing AI traffic across model providers and agent tools. It is worth evaluating for organizations that already use Envoy or need a customizable gateway within a cloud-native infrastructure stack. Explore Agent Router How to Choose the Right Agent Gateway The best agent gateway depends on how your agents communicate, which tools they need, and how much control your organization requires over their interactions. A gateway designed mainly for model routing may not provide the same capabilities as one built around MCP federation, A2A communication, or enterprise identity management. Identifying the protocols your applications use If your agents rely heavily on MCP servers, prioritize gateways with tool discovery, invocation controls, and authentication support. If your architecture includes multiple cooperating agents, check for A2A support and policies that govern agent-to-agent requests. Security and governance should also influence your decision** Look for granular permissions, identity-aware access, rate limits, audit logs, and visibility into tool usage. These capabilities become important as more agents gain access to internal APIs, customer data, and business systems. Deployment requirements can narrow the list further A managed service can reduce infrastructure maintenance, while an open-source, self-hosted gateway gives teams more control over configuration and deployment. Consider your existing cloud environment, Kubernetes setup, compliance requirements, and operational resources before choosing. Evaluate performance and total cost Agent workflows can generate multiple model and tool calls for a single task, so request overhead, retries, caching, and provider failover can affect both latency and spending. Test the gateway with realistic workloads and compare the cost of the gateway, infrastructure, model usage, and supporting services. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between an agent gateway and an LLM gateway? An LLM gateway primarily manages requests between applications and language models. It handles model routing, provider selection, authentication, rate limits, and usage monitoring. An agent gateway covers a broader set of interactions. It can govern communication between agents, tools, MCP servers, and model providers. Some platforms combine both capabilities, allowing teams to manage model requests and agent workflows through one infrastructure layer. Why do AI agents need a gateway? AI agents often access multiple tools, APIs, and services to complete tasks. Without centralized controls, each integration can introduce separate authentication, permission, monitoring, and security requirements. A gateway provides a shared enforcement point for these interactions. It helps teams manage tool access, apply policies, monitor requests, and maintain visibility into how agents use connected resources. What is the difference between MCP and A2A? MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools, resources, and prompts. It provides a common interface for agents to discover and use capabilities exposed by MCP servers. A2A (Agent2Agent) focuses on communication between independent AI agents. It allows agents to discover other agents, delegate tasks, and exchange information. Both protocols support different parts of an agentic architecture. Can an agent gateway secure access to internal APIs? Yes. An agent gateway can sit between agents and internal services, enforcing authentication, authorization, and access policies before requests reach backend resources. Depending on the platform, teams can expose existing APIs as MCP tools, restrict access to specific operations, and monitor requests. Backend services should still enforce their own authorization and data-access rules, since gateway policies are one layer of a broader security architecture. Should I choose an open-source or managed agent gateway? An open-source gateway is a good choice when your team needs deployment flexibility, infrastructure control, and the ability to customize its configuration. It can also reduce software licensing costs, although your team remains responsible for hosting, maintenance, and operations. A managed gateway can reduce operational overhead and integrate with an existing cloud ecosystem. It may be a better fit when your organization prefers a provider-managed service and already relies on that provider's identity, networking, and monitoring tools. Final Thoughts Agent gateways are becoming an important part of production AI infrastructure as applications gain access to more tools, services, and other agents. They give engineering teams a central place to manage communication, enforce access policies, monitor usage, and maintain control over increasingly complex agent workflows. The nine platforms in this comparison address different needs. Bifrost covers LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic in a single open-source gateway, with enterprise governance and in-VPC, on-premises, or air-gapped deployment. Agent Router and IBM ContextForge are also worth evaluating for open-source deployments. Kong and Gravitee offer broader API management and agent governance capabilities, while Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, Google Cloud Agent Gateway, and Azure AI Gateway fit naturally into their respective cloud ecosystems. MuleSoft Agent Fabric provides enterprise agent discovery, orchestration, and governance. Before choosing, test the gateway against your actual agent workflows. Check how it handles tool permissions, identity, protocol support, request volume, and failure scenarios. Teams evaluating AI gateways can request a Bifrost demo or review the open-source repository. content_html_zh:
AI agents are becoming part of everyday software systems. They call APIs, retrieve information through MCP servers, use external tools, and delegate tasks to other agents. As these workflows become more capable, controlling what an agent can access and what it can do becomes a serious engineering concern, and it is the problem an agent gateway is built to solve.

An agent might need access to a customer database, an internal API, and an external model provider during the same workflow. Without a central control layer, teams can end up managing authentication, permissions, logging, and traffic policies across several independent integrations. That makes security reviews harder and leaves platform teams with limited visibility into what their agents are doing.

An agent gateway provides a shared layer for managing these interactions. It can authenticate agents, control access to tools, route requests, enforce policies, and record activity across agent-to-tool, agent-to-model, and agent-to-agent communication.

This guide compares nine agent gateways, including open-source projects, enterprise platforms, and managed cloud services. We'll look at their architecture, agent connectivity, security controls, deployment options, and pricing to help engineering teams identify the right fit for their AI infrastructure.

TL;DR

The best agent gateway depends on the protocols your agents use, the level of control your organization needs, and where you plan to run the gateway.

  • Bifrost: An open-source Go gateway for governing model requests, MCP tool calls, and agent-to-agent (A2A) traffic, with virtual keys, usage budgets, access controls, and low request overhead.
  • MuleSoft Agent Fabric: An enterprise platform for discovering, governing, and orchestrating AI agents, with centralized control over agent interactions, MCP connectivity, and A2A communication.
  • Kong AI Gateway: Extends Kong's API management platform with AI and agent traffic capabilities, including MCP access controls and agent-to-agent connectivity.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: A managed AWS gateway that exposes APIs, Lambda functions, and existing services as tools for agents, with authentication and routing for agentic traffic.
  • Google Cloud Agent Gateway: A managed gateway for governing agent communication over MCP, A2A, REST, and gRPC, with identity-aware access policies.
  • Azure AI Gateway: A Microsoft gateway for managing model APIs and MCP tools through centralized identity, policy enforcement, networking, and observability.
  • Gravitee: An API management platform with AI and agent gateway capabilities for governing LLM requests, MCP servers, and agent interactions.
  • IBM ContextForge: An open-source MCP gateway and registry for discovering, securing, and managing tools and services exposed to AI agents.
  • Agent Router: An open-source, Envoy-based gateway for routing AI and agent traffic across model providers, self-hosted inference, and MCP services.

Some of these products are purpose-built for agent traffic, while others extend existing API management or cloud infrastructure platforms. That distinction matters when comparing their features, deployment models, and licensing.

What Is an Agent Gateway, and Why Does It Matter?

An agent gateway is an infrastructure layer between AI agents and the resources they interact with. Those resources can include language models, APIs, MCP servers, databases, internal services, and other agents.

When an agent performs a task, it may make several calls across different systems. Each interaction can involve a different credential, permission level, protocol, or security requirement. An agent gateway gives platform teams a central place to manage those interactions and apply consistent controls.

Depending on the implementation, an agent gateway can provide:

  • Agent authentication and identity: Identify which agent is making a request and verify its credentials.
  • Tool access control: Restrict which MCP tools, APIs, and services an agent can invoke.
  • MCP traffic management: Route and govern requests between agents and Model Context Protocol servers.
  • Agent-to-agent communication: Manage interactions between agents using protocols such as A2A.
  • Model routing: Direct model requests to configured providers or inference services.
  • Observability and audit logs: Track tool calls, model requests, policy decisions, and agent activity.
  • Traffic and usage policies: Apply rate limits, quotas, and other controls to agent requests.

These capabilities become important when agents have access to business-critical systems. A permissions mistake can expose sensitive information, while an unmonitored tool call can trigger an unexpected operation or incur costs that are difficult to attribute.

An agent gateway helps establish a consistent security and governance layer around these interactions. It does not replace application-level authorization or make an agent inherently safe, but it gives infrastructure teams a central point to enforce and monitor important policies.

How We Evaluated These Agent Gateways

This comparison focuses on how well each platform handles the infrastructure requirements of real agentic applications. We considered the following criteria:

  • Agent and protocol support: Compatibility with MCP, A2A, model APIs, and other agent communication patterns.
  • Security and governance: Authentication, agent identity, authorization, tool-level permissions, and audit capabilities.
  • Traffic management: Routing, access policies, rate limits, quotas, and failure handling.
  • Deployment and integration: Self-hosted, managed, cloud-native, and enterprise deployment options.
  • Open-source availability and pricing: Which components are open source, what requires a commercial plan, and the operational costs involved.

The comparison distinguishes between products built specifically for agent connectivity and broader API or cloud platforms that provide agent gateway functionality.

Quick Comparison: 9 Best Agent Gateways

The table gives you a starting point for comparing the nine platforms. Open-source status refers to the gateway project or core, not necessarily every commercial feature offered by its provider.

The products differ in what they govern. Some focus on securing tool access and MCP connections, while others also handle model routing and agent-to-agent communication. The following sections discuss those differences in more detail.

1. Bifrost (by Maxim AI)

Bifrost is an open-source AI gateway built in Go that also provides MCP gateway and agent gateway capabilities. It gives AI applications and agents a unified interface for accessing model providers and external tools, with centralized routing, authentication, usage controls, and observability.

For teams building agentic applications, one of Bifrost's important capabilities is its MCP integration. Agents can access external tools through a managed gateway, while engineering teams control which tools are available and how requests are governed. Bifrost also supports more than 20 model providers through a consistent API, making it useful for applications that combine model calls with external tool execution.

MCP Gateway and Agent Tool Governance

An AI agent often needs access to several tools to complete a task. Managing those connections independently can make it difficult to enforce consistent permissions across applications and teams.

Bifrost provides an MCP gateway that connects agents to external MCP servers and applies centralized controls to tool access. Its virtual keys can define which MCP clients and tools an agent is allowed to use, giving teams a way to restrict access at the gateway level.

Key capabilities include:

  • MCP tool filtering: Control which tools are available to individual virtual keys.
  • Centralized tool access: Connect agents to external MCP servers through a managed gateway.
  • Federated authentication: Support authenticated access to internal APIs exposed through MCP.
  • MCP Code Mode: Let agents interact with multiple tools through code execution, reducing the overhead associated with handling large tool definitions and repeated calls.

This approach is useful when several agents or applications share the same internal tools but need different access permissions.

Agent Gateway (A2A)

Bifrost also provides a dedicated A2A Agent Gateway for managing communication between AI agents. Teams can register existing A2A agents and control which callers are allowed to reach each one, creating a centralized access layer for agent-to-agent interactions.

The gateway also supports credential forwarding and push notifications, helping agents communicate with existing services while preserving the authentication context required by those integrations. Bifrost links A2A tasks with their corresponding LLM and MCP logs, giving teams a more complete view of agent workflows.

For observability, agent telemetry can also be exported through OpenTelemetry, making it easier to monitor A2A activity alongside other AI traffic.

Performance, Routing, and Reliability

Agent workflows can generate several model and tool requests during a single user interaction. Gateway overhead can accumulate across those calls, making request performance an important infrastructure consideration.

Bifrost is written in Go and is designed to handle high-throughput AI traffic with low overhead. It adds 11 microseconds of overhead per request at 5,000 requests per second (RPS) on a t3.xlarge instance, with a 100% success rate in sustained benchmarks.

For production agent systems, Bifrost provides:

  • Automatic failover: Redirect requests when a configured provider becomes unavailable.
  • Adaptive load balancing: Distribute traffic across configured providers and API keys.
  • Retries and circuit breakers: Handle transient errors and provider degradation.
  • Semantic caching: Reuse eligible responses to reduce repeated model requests.

These capabilities help teams maintain predictable model access as agent workloads increase.

Observability, Access Control, and Cost Governance

When agents interact with internal services and external tools, teams need visibility into both AI consumption and the permissions granted to each application.

Bifrost uses virtual keys as a central governance mechanism. Each key can carry its own model access permissions, budget, and rate limits, allowing teams to associate AI usage with specific applications, customers, or workloads.

Its governance capabilities include:

  • Independent budgets: Set spending limits for individual virtual keys.
  • Rate limits: Apply token-based and request-based restrictions.
  • Model and provider filtering: Restrict which models and provider credentials a key can access.
  • MCP permissions: Control which configured tools are available to a key.
  • Observability: Use built-in dashboards and OpenTelemetry support to monitor AI traffic.

This gives platform teams a way to manage model usage and agent tool permissions through the same gateway infrastructure.

Pricing:

Bifrost's core gateway is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and can be self-hosted without a gateway license fee. Teams remain responsible for infrastructure costs and charges from the model providers they use.

Its Enterprise offering adds advanced capabilities such as RBAC, SSO, guardrails, audit logs, and private deployment options, including in-VPC, on-premises, and air-gapped environments.

Best for:

Engineering and platform teams building production AI agents that need centralized MCP tool governance, low-overhead model access, and control over usage across applications. It is a strong fit for organizations that want LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic governed through one low-overhead gateway, with self-hosted, in-VPC, or air-gapped deployment.

Explore Bifrost

2. MuleSoft Agent Fabric

MuleSoft Agent Fabric is an enterprise platform for discovering, managing, and governing AI agents across an organization. It brings agent management and orchestration into the broader MuleSoft ecosystem, helping teams connect agents with enterprise APIs, systems, and business processes.

A central part of the platform is its approach to agent governance. Organizations can discover and register agents, manage their interactions, and apply governance policies across agent environments. Its support for MCP and A2A helps connect agents with tools and services while enabling communication between different agents.

MuleSoft Agent Fabric is designed for enterprises that need visibility and control as agent deployments grow across teams and business units. Its integration with MuleSoft's API management and connectivity capabilities also makes it relevant for organizations that already use MuleSoft to expose and manage enterprise services.

Pricing:

MuleSoft Agent Fabric is part of Salesforce's commercial enterprise platform. Pricing depends on the products, capabilities, and deployment requirements selected. Contact Salesforce or MuleSoft for a quote.

Best for:

Large organizations managing multiple AI agents across enterprise systems that need centralized discovery, governance, orchestration, and integration with existing APIs.

Explore MuleSoft Agent Fabric

3. Kong AI Gateway

Kong AI Gateway extends Kong's API connectivity and management platform to cover AI applications and multi-agent systems. It provides a centralized layer for governing LLM requests, MCP tool access, and agent-to-agent communication.

One of its main advantages is that it brings AI traffic management into an established API gateway ecosystem. Teams can expose existing APIs as MCP tools, aggregate tools from different sources, and apply authentication and access policies to how agents discover and invoke them.

Kong also supports A2A traffic through dedicated AI Agent entities. These allow teams to route agent requests and apply authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and observability policies. Administrators can monitor agent activity, including request latency, errors, and other telemetry, through Kong's management and observability capabilities.

For organizations already using Kong to manage APIs, this creates a familiar path to governing agent infrastructure without introducing a completely separate connectivity platform.

Pricing:

Kong offers an AI Management Plus plan starting at $25 per month, plus usage, with a free trial. Its Enterprise plan uses custom pricing and adds capabilities for larger deployments.

Best for:

Organizations already using Kong for API management, as well as enterprises that need centralized governance across LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic. It is especially relevant when agents need controlled access to existing enterprise APIs and services.

Explore Kong AI Gateway

4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is a managed gateway service designed to connect AI agents with tools, APIs, and existing services. It helps developers expose backend capabilities through a standardized interface that agents can discover and invoke using the Model Context Protocol.

A key use case is turning existing REST APIs, AWS Lambda functions, and other services into MCP-compatible tools. This allows teams to make existing business logic available to agents without building a separate tool integration for every application. AgentCore Gateway can also connect to existing MCP servers and support agent-to-agent communication through passthrough targets.

Because it is part of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the gateway fits naturally into AWS-based agent architectures. Teams can use it alongside other AgentCore capabilities to build and operate agents that interact with enterprise systems and external services.

The managed approach also reduces the infrastructure work involved in running a dedicated gateway. Developers can focus on configuring targets, permissions, and agent integrations while AWS manages the underlying service.

Pricing:

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway uses pay-as-you-go pricing. AWS lists gateway API invocations at $0.005 per 1,000 invocations, with additional charges for features such as search and tool indexing. Other AgentCore services and the AWS resources used by connected tools can generate separate costs.

Best for:

Teams building agents within the AWS ecosystem that need a managed way to expose APIs, Lambda functions, and existing services as MCP tools. It is a practical option for organizations that want to integrate agent capabilities with their existing AWS infrastructure.

Explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

5. Google Cloud Agent Gateway

Google Cloud Agent Gateway is a managed gateway within Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It provides a centralized layer for securing and governing communication between AI agents, tools, and backend services across cloud environments.

The gateway supports several agent communication protocols, including MCP, A2A, REST, and gRPC. This allows organizations to manage tool calls, agent delegation, and traditional service requests through a consistent gateway infrastructure. For MCP traffic, it can inspect JSON-RPC requests to identify tool names and methods, enabling more granular access policies.

Google Cloud Agent Gateway is designed for organizations that need to govern agent interactions across different deployment environments. It supports deployments involving Google Kubernetes Engine and Cloud Run, as well as cross-cloud scenarios. Its integration with Google Cloud's agent infrastructure also makes it relevant for teams already using Gemini and other Google Cloud services.

Pricing:

Google Cloud Agent Gateway is part of the managed Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Pricing depends on the selected deployment model and associated platform resources.

Best for:

Organizations building agents on Google Cloud that need centralized control over MCP tools, A2A communication, and backend service access. It is a strong option for teams managing agent workloads across GKE, Cloud Run, and hybrid or cross-cloud environments.

Explore Google Cloud Agent Gateway

6. Azure AI Gateway

Azure AI Gateway is Microsoft's managed gateway for connecting applications and AI agents to model providers, MCP servers, and other tools. It gives developers a shared endpoint for AI services while allowing platform teams to manage access, policies, networking, and observability centrally.

The gateway supports multiple model providers through familiar API interfaces, helping applications work with different models without requiring a separate integration for each provider. It can also publish MCP servers, OpenAPI APIs, and SaaS connectors through a unified MCP endpoint, making approved tools available to agents through a governed access layer.

For enterprise environments, Azure AI Gateway provides policies for access control, safety, token usage, and request rates. Its monitoring capabilities expose information such as token consumption, latency, errors, and policy outcomes. Integration with Azure identity and networking services also makes it suitable for organizations with established Microsoft security and infrastructure requirements.

Pricing:

Azure AI Gateway is currently offered as a preview service. Microsoft has not announced final pricing for the separate Azure API Management AI Gateway tier.

Best for:

Enterprises using Microsoft Azure that need a shared gateway for model APIs and MCP tools. It is especially useful for platform teams that want consistent identity, security policies, and monitoring across AI applications.

Explore Azure AI Gateway

7. Gravitee AI Gateway

Gravitee AI Gateway is part of Gravitee's API and agent management platform. It provides a unified runtime for governing LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic, helping organizations secure interactions across agents, models, tools, and existing APIs.

Gravitee separates these interactions into protocol-aware gateway components. Its LLM Proxy manages model requests, while its MCP Proxy controls tool discovery and invocation. The A2A Proxy governs communication between agents, including delegated requests and authorization across agent workflows.

A key distinction is its focus on fine-grained governance. Teams can apply policies to specific MCP methods, tools, and agent skills, with OAuth 2.1 authentication and delegated authorization support. Gravitee also connects observability across these interactions through OpenTelemetry, giving teams visibility into agent identities, tool usage, policy decisions, and request traces.

The platform also includes MCP Studio, which helps teams assemble composite MCP servers from existing APIs, tools, and other resources. This allows organizations to provide agents with curated tool collections while applying access policies at the composite level.

Pricing:

Gravitee offers commercial platform plans with pricing based on deployment requirements and selected capabilities. Its AI Gateway capabilities are part of its broader platform offering. Contact Gravitee for a quote and confirmation of the features available under each plan.

Best for:

Enterprises that need detailed governance across LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic. Gravitee is a good fit for organizations managing many agents and tools that require centralized authentication, fine-grained authorization, and end-to-end observability.

8. IBM ContextForge

IBM ContextForge is an open-source MCP gateway and registry designed to help organizations manage tools, resources, and prompts across multiple MCP servers. It provides a centralized layer where AI agents can discover and access approved capabilities without requiring every application to maintain separate connections to individual services.

ContextForge supports MCP server federation, allowing teams to register and aggregate tools from different sources through a unified endpoint. It also provides authentication and authorization mechanisms, including OAuth-based access, JWT authentication, and role-based access control. Administrators can manage tool visibility, control access, and monitor interactions across connected services.

The platform also includes an administrative interface and observability integrations that help teams manage their MCP infrastructure. Its focus is on organizing and governing tool access, making it useful for organizations with growing MCP deployments that need a shared registry and gateway.

Pricing:

IBM ContextForge is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and can be self-hosted without a software license fee. Organizations can use their own infrastructure and configure the gateway according to their requirements.

Best for:

Teams building MCP-based agent environments that need a centralized tool registry, server federation, and access management. It is a practical option for organizations that prefer open-source infrastructure and want control over their MCP deployments.

9. Agent Router

Agent Router is an open-source gateway built on Envoy that helps teams manage traffic across AI models, agents, and tools. It provides a unified routing layer for applications that interact with multiple model providers and agent infrastructure.

The gateway is designed to simplify connectivity across different AI backends, including hosted model APIs and self-hosted inference services. It also supports MCP integration, allowing agent applications to connect with external tools through a centralized infrastructure layer.

By using Envoy as its underlying proxy, Agent Router fits into cloud-native environments where teams already rely on service proxies and infrastructure-level traffic management. This makes it relevant for platform engineers who want to bring AI traffic into their existing networking and observability architecture.

Pricing:

Agent Router is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Teams can self-host it without paying a software license fee, although infrastructure and operational costs still apply.

Best for:

Engineering teams that want an open-source, Envoy-based gateway for routing AI traffic across model providers and agent tools. It is worth evaluating for organizations that already use Envoy or need a customizable gateway within a cloud-native infrastructure stack.

How to Choose the Right Agent Gateway

The best agent gateway depends on how your agents communicate, which tools they need, and how much control your organization requires over their interactions. A gateway designed mainly for model routing may not provide the same capabilities as one built around MCP federation, A2A communication, or enterprise identity management.

  • Identifying the protocols your applications use

If your agents rely heavily on MCP servers, prioritize gateways with tool discovery, invocation controls, and authentication support. If your architecture includes multiple cooperating agents, check for A2A support and policies that govern agent-to-agent requests.

  • Security and governance should also influence your decision**

Look for granular permissions, identity-aware access, rate limits, audit logs, and visibility into tool usage. These capabilities become important as more agents gain access to internal APIs, customer data, and business systems.

  • Deployment requirements can narrow the list further

A managed service can reduce infrastructure maintenance, while an open-source, self-hosted gateway gives teams more control over configuration and deployment. Consider your existing cloud environment, Kubernetes setup, compliance requirements, and operational resources before choosing.

  • Evaluate performance and total cost

Agent workflows can generate multiple model and tool calls for a single task, so request overhead, retries, caching, and provider failover can affect both latency and spending. Test the gateway with realistic workloads and compare the cost of the gateway, infrastructure, model usage, and supporting services.

常见问题解答

What is the difference between an agent gateway and an LLM gateway?
An LLM gateway primarily manages requests between applications and language models. It handles model routing, provider selection, authentication, rate limits, and usage monitoring.
An agent gateway covers a broader set of interactions. It can govern communication between agents, tools, MCP servers, and model providers. Some platforms combine both capabilities, allowing teams to manage model requests and agent workflows through one infrastructure layer.
Why do AI agents need a gateway?
AI agents often access multiple tools, APIs, and services to complete tasks. Without centralized controls, each integration can introduce separate authentication, permission, monitoring, and security requirements.
A gateway provides a shared enforcement point for these interactions. It helps teams manage tool access, apply policies, monitor requests, and maintain visibility into how agents use connected resources.
What is the difference between MCP and A2A?
MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools, resources, and prompts. It provides a common interface for agents to discover and use capabilities exposed by MCP servers.
A2A (Agent2Agent) focuses on communication between independent AI agents. It allows agents to discover other agents, delegate tasks, and exchange information. Both protocols support different parts of an agentic architecture.
Can an agent gateway secure access to internal APIs?
Yes. An agent gateway can sit between agents and internal services, enforcing authentication, authorization, and access policies before requests reach backend resources.
Depending on the platform, teams can expose existing APIs as MCP tools, restrict access to specific operations, and monitor requests. Backend services should still enforce their own authorization and data-access rules, since gateway policies are one layer of a broader security architecture.
Should I choose an open-source or managed agent gateway?
An open-source gateway is a good choice when your team needs deployment flexibility, infrastructure control, and the ability to customize its configuration. It can also reduce software licensing costs, although your team remains responsible for hosting, maintenance, and operations.
A managed gateway can reduce operational overhead and integrate with an existing cloud ecosystem. It may be a better fit when your organization prefers a provider-managed service and already relies on that provider's identity, networking, and monitoring tools.

Agent gateways are becoming an important part of production AI infrastructure as applications gain access to more tools, services, and other agents. They give engineering teams a central place to manage communication, enforce access policies, monitor usage, and maintain control over increasingly complex agent workflows.

The nine platforms in this comparison address different needs.
